new_statements.rule_in_words: Taiwan Sign Language is a signed language, so the catalog's positional word-stress classes (initial/penult/weight etc.) do not apply. The only explicit statement about 'word stress' in TSL found in any opened source is Smith's own summary of his 1981 working paper: word stress or emphasis is one of six functions accompanied by eyebrow raising (a nonmanual marker); no locus or rule within the sign is given. Duncan 2005: 310 adds, tentatively, that slowed, deliberate signing may be the TSL analogue of prosodic lengthening/emphasis at discourse level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Related timing fact (Smith 2005: 196, from Smith 1982a): in TSL compounds the first member is shorter than the second and both are shorter than in isolation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level emphasis ('word stress or emphasis') and clause/discourse-level prominence; based on Smith's videotaped native-signer data (Taipei/Tainan varieties). Statement is the author's own retrospective summary of an unpublished 1981 working paper, not a phonological analysis of stress placement. Confidence 'medium' reflects a clear quote in an open first-hand source but a category mismatch with spoken-language stress typology.
new_statements.identity_note: Taiwan Sign Language (taiw1241, ISO tss), a signed language of the Japanese Sign Language family; Smith's data come from native signers of the Taipei and Tainan varieties (both TSL). Word-stress placement categories are inapplicable to a signed language; recommend catalog treatment as 'not applicable (signed language)' rather than as a stress-system entry.

sources.quote: 2.14 Smith (1981b) was a more detailed look at the function of eyebrow raising in TSL. I noted that brow raising was used in conjunction with the following phenomena: (1) yes-no questions, (2) topicalizations, (3) affect, (4) if-clauses and appositions, (5) word stress or emphasis, and (6) to mark sentence breaks and boundaries.
sources.note: p. 195-196, summarising the author's own Smith 1981b working paper: eyebrow raising in TSL co-occurs with six phenomena including '(5) word stress or emphasis'; also (p. 196, Smith 1982a) first member of a compound is shorter than the second and all signs shorten in compounds. No positional stress rule (signed language). Sec. 3.1 lists 'timing of segments' among open phonological questions.
Nothing on phonology/stress; only nonmanual markers listed. Reference list yielded Smith 2005 and Fischer & Gong 2010.
